newsitem.title: USA: Florida hopes to have Liggett documents.
newsitem.headline: Florida hopes to have Liggett documents.

text.p: Florida attorneys said Friday they expected to get their hands on some contested Liggett Group Inc. documents within a week, following an appeals court ruling Friday giving the tobacco attorneys until Tuesday to seek a rehearing on their release.
"This is great news, great news," said W.C. Gentry, one of Florida's lead attorneys in its Medicaid case against tobacco firms.
On Wednesday, Florida's 4th District Court of Appeal upheld a ruling allowing the state to use documents obtained by Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett in its lawsuit.

The ruling was a defeat for tobacco companies, which had claimed the documents were protected by attorney-client privilege. Attorneys for the state had successfully argued that the documents were exempt from that privilege because they involved alleged plans to commit a crime or fraud.
The ruling involves 13 Liggett documents dating from 1963 to 1988.
On Friday morning, the appellate court gave tobacco companies until Tuesday to seek a rehearing.

Gentry said it was unlikely the appeal court would reverse its Wednesday ruling. Under Florida law, he said, the decision could not appealed to the Florida Supreme Court, "which means we should have the documents in our hands by Friday," he said.
Stephen Krigbaum, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., said the tobacco companies were prepared to file their response for rehearing by Tuesday.
But he added, "It appears that the court is preparing to make some new law (in the area of attorney-client privilege)."
On Friday, Philip Morris also lost its bid to keep more than 400 of its company documents from being introduced at trial on grounds they had not been found to be bona fide.

During a hearing before William Rutter, the special magistrate appointed for the case, Gentry pointed out that Philip Morris had been "dragging its feet for months" regarding to authentication of the documents.
"They (Philip Morris) shouldn't be allowed to continue playing this game," Gentry said.

Rutter ruled Friday the documents were bona fide over Philip Morris's objections. He also gave Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. until Tuesday to either authenticate or deny some 60 of its documents that are in the archives of the University of California.
